title: Standard precautions and hand hygiene
blurb: Apply the 10 standard infection control precautions to every person, and choose the right hand hygiene at the right moment.
question: A nurse has just helped Mr Okafor, who has suspected Clostridioides difficile diarrhoea, back to bed from the commode. She removes her gloves and apron. How should she decontaminate her hands?

teach.h: Standard precautions: every person, every time
teach.body: Standard infection control precautions (SICPs) are the basic measures that stop infection spreading from recognised AND unrecognised sources. The National IPC Manual says they are used by all staff, in all care settings, at all times, for all patients, whether or not infection is known to be present. In plain English: you cannot tell who is carrying an organism, so treat blood, body fluids, secretions, excretions (not sweat), broken skin and mucous membranes as potentially infectious every time.
teach.cite: NHS England National IPC Manual (NIPCM), chapter 1

teach.caption: Hand hygiene is described in the NIPCM as one of the most important ways to reduce healthcare associated infection.

items: Bare below the elbows: expose your forearms (disposable over-sleeves worn for religious reasons are removed before hand hygiene and replaced after).
Remove hand and wrist jewellery. A single plain metal ring, such as a wedding band, is allowed but is moved during hand hygiene.
A religious bangle can be pushed up the forearm during hand hygiene and secured during care.
Keep nails short and clean, with no artificial nails or nail products.
Cover cuts and abrasions with a waterproof dressing.

teach.h: The five moments for hand hygiene
teach.caption: Also before putting on and after removing gloves. Moments 1 and 2 protect the patient; moments 3 to 5 protect you and the environment.

teach.h: Soap and water or alcohol handrub?

rows.label: Use when
values: Hands visibly soiled; vomiting or diarrhoea; suspected or known GI infection
All other routine hand hygiene during direct care

teach.caption: Alcohol does not reliably remove C. difficile spores or norovirus, so friction and rinsing with soap and water are needed.

teach.body: Coverage matters more than product: palms, backs of hands, between the fingers, backs of fingers, thumbs, fingertips and wrists. Dry hands thoroughly with disposable paper towels after washing. Use an emollient hand cream regularly, for example on breaks and off duty, but not from communal tubs. Staff with skin problems should seek advice from occupational health or their GP, because damaged skin harbours organisms and is harder to clean.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Nurse Priya and Mr Okafor
teach.body: Priya helps Mr Okafor, 78, who has suspected C. difficile diarrhoea, back from the commode. She removes her gloves and apron inside his room and washes her hands with liquid soap and running water, then dries them with paper towels. Handrub would not reliably remove spores. Before leaving she also makes sure the commode is decontaminated. Later, before checking another patient's cannula, she uses handrub (moment 2) because her hands are clean.

teach.caption: Hand hygiene also matters outside direct care: start and end of shift, entering and leaving clinical areas, before eating and after using the toilet.

teach.text: Gloves are NOT a substitute for hand hygiene, and gloves are never washed or rubbed with handrub between tasks. Decontaminate hands before putting gloves on and after taking them off. And remember the classic: handrub is fine for MRSA, but C. difficile and norovirus need soap and water.

items: SICPs apply to all staff, all settings, all patients, at all times, whether or not infection is known.
Bare below the elbows; one plain metal ring; short nails, no artificial nails; cover cuts.
Five moments: before patient, before clean or aseptic task, after body fluid risk, after patient, after surroundings.
Soap and water for visible soiling, vomiting or diarrhoea, C. difficile and norovirus; otherwise alcohol handrub.
Protect your skin: dry thoroughly, use your own emollient, report skin problems.

summary: You can now list the 10 standard infection control precautions and explain why they apply to everyone. You can also choose between soap and water and alcohol handrub, apply the five moments and protect your own skin.

A.q: During induction, a healthcare assistant asks the nurse which patients standard infection control precautions should be used for. Which reply is correct?
options: All patients, whether or not infection is known
Patients admitted with diarrhoea, rash or fever
Patients with a confirmed infection or colonisation
Patients who are immunosuppressed or frail
A.why: The NIPCM states SICPs are used by all staff, in all care settings, at all times, for all patients whether infection is known to be present or not, because many sources are unrecognised.

whyNot.1: These symptoms flag a cross-infection risk for placement, but SICPs are not limited to them.
whyNot.2: Known infection may need transmission-based precautions on top, but SICPs are the baseline for everyone.
whyNot.3: Vulnerable patients benefit, but SICPs protect every patient, staff member and visitor.

A.q: Nurse Callum arrives for a shift on a medical ward wearing a wristwatch, a plain gold wedding band and gel nail varnish. What must he change before giving care?
options: Keep the watch on and remove the wedding band and nail gel
Remove the watch and the nail gel, and keep the plain wedding band
Remove the wedding band, and keep the watch pinned to his tunic sleeve
Keep the nail gel, and remove the watch and the wedding band
A.why: Staff must remove wrist jewellery and must not wear artificial nails or nail products. A single plain metal ring is permitted but is moved during hand hygiene (NIPCM 1.2).

whyNot.0: The watch prevents effective wrist decontamination, and the plain band is allowed.
whyNot.2: The plain band did not need to come off, and the nail gel, which is not permitted, would still be left on.
whyNot.3: Nail products are not allowed, and the plain wedding band is permitted.

A.q: A nurse straightens the bed sheets and moves the water jug of Mrs Adeyemi, who is asleep. The nurse does not touch her. Which moment for hand hygiene now applies?
options: Before touching a patient
After body fluid exposure risk
Before a clean or aseptic procedure
After touching her surroundings
A.why: Touching the bed linen and jug is contact with the patient's immediate surroundings, which can carry the same organisms as the patient: moment 5.

whyNot.0: No patient contact is about to happen; the contact has already been with her surroundings.
whyNot.1: There was no contact with blood or body fluids.
whyNot.2: No clean or aseptic task is being started.

B.q: Mr Hussain, 70, has vomiting and diarrhoea and suspected norovirus. After assisting him with personal care and removing her gloves and apron, what should the nurse use to decontaminate her hands?
options: Alcohol-based handrub for 20 to 30 seconds
An antiseptic hand wipe, followed by alcohol handrub
Liquid soap and running water, then paper towels
Alcohol handrub, then a further application
B.why: The NIPCM specifies liquid soap and water when caring for patients with vomiting or diarrhoea or suspected or known GI infection such as norovirus.

whyNot.0: Alcohol handrub is not reliable against norovirus; soap and water is specified here.
whyNot.1: Hand wipes then handrub are a stopgap when running water is unavailable, not the standard where a basin exists.
whyNot.3: Repeating handrub does not overcome its poor action against norovirus.

B.q: A student nurse uses alcohol handrub for about 10 seconds, rubbing palms together, then dries her hands on her tunic. What is the most important correction?
options: Use soap and water for every hand hygiene moment
Rinse the handrub off and dry with paper towels
Apply a second dose of handrub after the first one
Cover every surface and rub for 20 to 30 seconds
B.why: Effective handrubbing covers every surface, including thumbs, fingertips and between the fingers, for 20 to 30 seconds until the hands are dry (WHO technique, NIPCM appendix 2).

whyNot.0: Handrub is the routine method for clean hands; soap and water is for specific situations.
whyNot.1: Handrub is not rinsed; it works as it dries on the skin.
whyNot.2: A second dose with the same poor technique still misses surfaces.

B.q: Staff nurse Ben has red, cracked skin on both hands after weeks of frequent hand hygiene. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Wear gloves for all care to rest the skin
Use his own emollient and seek occupational health advice
Switch from handrub to soap and water for all moments
Use the communal ward tub of hand cream between each patient
B.why: The NIPCM advises regular emollient use (on breaks and off duty), no communal tubs, and occupational health or GP advice for skin problems.

whyNot.0: Unnecessary glove use is discouraged and does not replace hand hygiene; occlusion can worsen skin.
whyNot.2: Frequent washing is generally harsher on skin than handrub, and handrub remains the routine method.
whyNot.3: Communal tubs of hand cream should not be used in care settings because they can become contaminated.

C.q: On a busy surgical ward, a nurse has just emptied a catheter bag for Mr Lee, then removes her gloves. She next needs to flush the peripheral cannula of Mrs Clarke in the next bed. Her hands look clean. What should she do?
options: Wash with soap and water, then use handrub as well, then flush the cannula
Put on a new pair of gloves straight away and flush the cannula
Perform hand hygiene after removing gloves and again before the flush
Use handrub once after reaching Mrs Clarke and before touching her
C.why: Hand hygiene is needed after glove removal and body fluid exposure risk (moment 3), and again before touching Mrs Clarke and before the aseptic task (moments 1 and 2). Clean hands mean handrub is suitable.

whyNot.0: Soap and water is not required for visibly clean hands without GI infection, and doing both adds nothing.
whyNot.1: New gloves without hand hygiene carry organisms from Mr Lee to Mrs Clarke; gloves do not replace hand hygiene.
whyNot.3: A single handrub at Mrs Clarke's bed misses the hand hygiene needed immediately after glove removal and before touching the surroundings in between.

C.q: A community nurse visits Mrs Bowen at home and finds there is no running water while she is changing a heavily soiled dressing. Her hands are visibly soiled. What should she do?
options: Use hand wipes, then handrub, and wash at the first opportunity
Use alcohol handrub and continue the visit
Leave the hands as they are and wash at the next visit
Use handrub twice, then put on sterile gloves to continue the visit
C.why: The NIPCM allows hand wipes followed by alcohol handrub where hand washing is indicated but running water is unavailable, with hand washing at the first opportunity.

whyNot.1: Handrub alone is not effective on visibly soiled hands.
whyNot.2: Leaving soiled hands until the next visit risks cross-infection to the patient, the nurse and the next home.
whyNot.3: Handrub does not clean soiled hands, and sterile gloves do not replace hand hygiene.

C.q: A ward manager is auditing hand hygiene. Which observation shows correct practice?
options: A nurse rubs handrub over her gloves between two patients
A nurse in a long-sleeved cardigan rolls her sleeves to the wrist
A nurse decontaminates her hands before putting on gloves
A nurse skips hand hygiene because she wore gloves for the task
C.why: The NIPCM requires hand hygiene before putting on and after removing gloves.

whyNot.0: Gloves must never be decontaminated with handrub between uses; they are changed between patients and tasks.
whyNot.1: Bare below the elbows means forearms are exposed, not sleeves rolled to the wrist.
whyNot.3: Gloves are not a substitute for hand hygiene; hands must be decontaminated after glove removal.

reteach.title: Think of your hands as the delivery van
reteach.question: If organisms could only travel between patients by hitching a ride, what would they ride on most often?

blocks.body: Most cross-infection travels by contact, and staff hands are the commonest vehicle. Every time you move from a patient, their bed or a body fluid towards something clean (another person, a cannula, a clean tray), you must 'empty the van' with hand hygiene. Jewellery, watches, long sleeves and long or false nails are places where organisms hide, which is why you go bare below the elbows.

children.edge: Visibly soiled, or vomiting, diarrhoea, C. difficile, norovirus
children.label: Liquid soap and water

blocks.text: 'Gloves on' does not mean 'hands clean'. Hand hygiene before gloving and again after taking gloves off, every time.

explain.body: Ten precautions, used by all staff for all patients at all times. They protect against organisms nobody knows are there yet, which is why you never wait for a diagnosis before using them.

test.q: Why are standard infection control precautions used for patients with no known infection?
options: Because a laboratory diagnosis may take several days
Because patients expect to see them used
Because the law requires them in hospitals
Because many sources of infection are unrecognised
test.why: SICPs reduce transmission from both recognised and unrecognised sources of infection (NIPCM chapter 1).

whyNot.0: Waiting for a diagnosis is not the reason; many carriers are never diagnosed at all during a stay.
whyNot.1: Patient reassurance is not the purpose; protection from unrecognised sources is.
whyNot.2: SICPs apply in all care settings, not just hospitals, and the rationale is clinical risk.

explain.body: Forearms exposed, wrist jewellery off, one plain metal ring allowed but moved during hand hygiene, short clean nails with no artificial nails or products, and cuts covered with a waterproof dressing.

test.q: Which item may a nurse keep on while providing direct care?
options: A single plain metal ring
A fitness tracker on the wrist
A ring with a small stone
Clear nail varnish
test.why: The NIPCM permits a single plain metal finger ring, moved during hand hygiene.

whyNot.1: Wrist items must be removed so wrists can be decontaminated.
whyNot.2: Stones create crevices where organisms collect, so only a plain band is permitted.
whyNot.3: No nail products are allowed, including clear varnish.

explain.body: Before touching a patient; before clean or aseptic procedures; after body fluid exposure risk; after touching a patient; after touching a patient's immediate surroundings. Plus before gloving and after removing gloves.

test.q: A nurse is about to change the dressing over a central line. Which moment for hand hygiene does this represent?
options: After touching a patient
Before a clean or aseptic procedure
After body fluid exposure risk
After touching the patient's surroundings
test.why: Accessing or dressing an invasive device is a clean or aseptic procedure: moment 2, which protects the patient.

whyNot.0: This moment follows contact; here the task is about to begin.
whyNot.2: This follows contact with body fluids, not the start of an aseptic task.
whyNot.3: This follows contact with the bed space, not the start of a procedure.

explain.body: Liquid soap and water when hands are visibly soiled, with vomiting or diarrhoea, or with suspected or known GI infection such as norovirus or C. difficile. Alcohol handrub for everything else during direct care.

test.q: Mrs Grant has MRSA colonisation of a leg wound and no diarrhoea. After redressing it and removing gloves, the nurse's hands are visibly clean. Which method is appropriate?
options: Liquid soap and running water
An antiseptic surgical scrub
Alcohol-based handrub
Hand wipes followed by handrub
test.why: With visibly clean hands and no GI infection, alcohol handrub is the routine method; it is effective against MRSA.

whyNot.0: Soap and water is reserved for soiled hands and GI infections such as C. difficile and norovirus.
whyNot.1: Surgical scrubbing is for surgical and some invasive procedures, not routine care.
whyNot.3: Hand wipes are a fallback where running water is unavailable and washing is indicated.
